header.title: Learn
header.subtitle: Short lessons on reading the chart, managing risk and practising on paper.
frame: Education only. Nothing here tells you what to trade.
Practise every idea on paper before you use real money.

lessons.title: What price structure means
lessons.summary: Price moves in swings. The way the swings line up tells you whether the market trends or moves sideways.
points: In an uptrend each swing high and each swing low is higher than the one before.
In a downtrend each swing high and each swing low is lower than the one before.
When the swings overlap and go nowhere, the market is in a range.
Read the structure on closed bars only. A bar that is still forming can change.

lessons.title: Buyer areas and seller areas
lessons.summary: An area is a zone where price turned before. It is a band, not a single line.
points: A buyer area is a zone where buyers stepped in and price turned up.
A seller area is a zone where sellers stepped in and price turned down.
An area is stronger when price left it quickly and has not come back many times since.
Price can pass through an area. An area only tells you where to pay attention.

lessons.title: Pullbacks and the handover
lessons.summary: In a trend, price often comes back to an area before it moves on. What happens inside the area matters.
points: A pullback is a move against the trend that comes back toward an area.
A handover forms when the side that was pushing gives way inside the area.
Wait for the handover to complete on a closed bar. Early guesses are often wrong.
If price moves through the area and holds beyond it, the idea is no longer valid.

lessons.title: Timeframes work together
lessons.summary: A higher timeframe shows the bigger picture. A lower timeframe shows the detail inside it.
points: Start on the higher timeframe: is the market trending or in a range?
Find the area on that timeframe.
Move to the lower timeframe only to watch how price behaves inside the area.
When the two timeframes disagree, the higher one sets the context.

lessons.title: RSI divergence in plain words
lessons.summary: RSI shows how strongly price moved lately. A divergence is when price and RSI disagree.
points: Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. The push up is getting weaker.
Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low but RSI makes a higher low. The push down is getting weaker.
A divergence is evidence, not a signal on its own. Read it at an area, with the structure.
Divergence can last a long time in a strong trend.

lessons.title: Decide your risk before the trade
lessons.summary: Before you enter, know where your idea is wrong and how much you accept to lose if it is.
points: Every idea has a point where it is no longer valid. Find it on the chart before you enter.
Decide how much of your capital one trade may lose. Keep it small and the same every time.
Your lot size follows from those two answers, not from how sure you feel.
These are your own settings. ATP never sets them for you.

lessons.title: Your daily loss limit
lessons.summary: A daily loss limit protects you on a bad day. You choose it; ATP keeps to it.
points: Set the most you are willing to lose in one day.
When your losses reach it, new entries pause until the next day.
Closing a trade always works, even when new entries are paused.
A bad day is normal. The limit keeps one bad day from becoming a bad month.

lessons.title: Options carry extra risk
lessons.summary: Options move faster than shares and lose value as expiry comes closer.
points: Most individual traders in futures and options lose money. Learn on paper first.
Time works against an option holder: its value shrinks every day until expiry.
Liquidity matters. A wide gap between the bid and the ask costs you on every trade.
Know the lot size and the most you can lose before you plan the trade.

lessons.title: Why practise on paper first
lessons.summary: Paper trading uses real prices and pretend money. No order reaches your broker.
points: Paper trading shows how an idea behaves without putting money at risk.
Treat it like real money: the same lot size, the same risk, the same rules.
Run an idea for many trades before you judge it. A few trades say very little.
ATP is paper only today. Real-money trading is not switched on.

lessons.title: Review your paper trades
lessons.summary: The review is where you learn. Compare what you planned with what happened.
points: Look at each closed trade: did you follow your own rules?
Note the mistakes that repeat, not only the single bad trade.
Check how often your daily limit paused new entries, and why.
Change one setting at a time, then practise again.

lessons.title: How ATP works
lessons.summary: You connect a broker for prices, pick an idea, set your own settings and practise it on paper.
points: Connect your broker so ATP can read prices. Your broker login stays with your broker.
Pick an idea from the library, or build your own, and choose its settings.
Start a paper bot. It watches the market for the structure you chose.
When the structure appears, you get a signal in plain words. You decide what to do.

lessons.title: Signals describe structure, not advice
lessons.summary: A signal says what the structure of your own idea shows. It never tells you what to trade.
points: A signal comes only from an idea you chose and settings you set.
It describes the structure, for example: the pullback reached a seller area and a handover is forming.
You decide the trade, the lot size and the exit.
Past results never promise future results.
